screens.title: SD-WAN Data Plane and Forwarding
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll follow real user traffic as it leaves a branch PC, moves into the local edge router, travels encrypted across the underlay, and arrives at a remote site. You will learn the essential pieces that make that journey possible: how the edge router finds the remote TLOC, how IPsec tunnels are negotiated, why encapsulation wraps the original packet for safe travel, and how data policies steer traffic for performance or security. Understanding this flow is critical for troubleshooting and for designing policies that preserve application experience. For example, you’ll see why a route in the control plane alone is not enough — the underlay must also carry the TLOC IPs so an IPsec tunnel can be established. We’ll also preview typical issues such as underlay reachability failure, firewall ports blocking IKE or NAT traversal, and policy misapplication that can lead to black-holing. By the end you will be able to explain the end-to-end forwarding path, verify IPsec state with CLI commands, and reason about policy-driven path choices.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › SD-WAN Data Plane and Forwarding
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Data Plane and Forwarding

Follow a packet from branch host to data center, learn how IPsec, encapsulation, and data policies produce predictable, secure forwarding.

Why this matters: Visibility into the data plane lets you confirm that traffic actually moves where routing and policies intend — and quickly find where it stops.

Example: A voice call uses Application-Aware Routing to prefer MPLS when latency is low, otherwise it fails over to internet transport.

In this lesson
  • End-to-end packet flow and FIB decisions
  • IPsec tunnel negotiation and ESP protection
  • Encapsulation / decapsulation with TLOC IPs
  • Data policies: AAR, service chaining, QoS
Coming up
Hands-on CLI verification and common troubleshooting checks you can run on a cEdge to confirm tunnel and data plane health.
Visual Concept

Secure Overlay Fabric

Branch
Host 192.168.10.10 → cEdge TLOC 10.0.1.1
Underlay
Encrypted outer IP uses source and destination TLOC IPs; routed by the underlay just like normal IP
Data Center
cEdge decapsulates and forwards to final host on service-side VPN

Quick topics to guide your study
Tunnel Setup
IKE and ESP
Encapsulation
Outer IP uses TLOCs
Data Policies
AAR, service chaining

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace the full data plane path and explain why each step matters for secure, predictable forwarding. You will demonstrate understanding of IPsec tunnel establishment — how IKE negotiates keys and ESP protects packet integrity and confidentiality — and you will know how encapsulation uses TLOC IP addresses so the underlay can route encrypted traffic. You will also be able to read the device's forwarding information base and explain how an OMP-learned route becomes a next-hop TLOC in the FIB. Finally you will be comfortable describing how data policies influence live forwarding decisions, for example preferring an MPLS TLOC for low-latency voice or steering traffic through a firewall for inspection. Each objective ties to practical verification steps you can run on a cEdge to confirm that the overlay and tunnels are healthy.

screens.title: End-to-end Data Plane Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Start by picturing a host packet in a branch LAN that needs to reach a remote server in a data center VPN. The local cEdge receives the original packet and must determine how to forward it. That decision comes from the Forwarding Information Base, which maps destination prefixes to next-hop TLOC addresses learned from OMP via the control plane. The router looks up the prefix, selects the corresponding TLOC, and checks whether an IPsec tunnel to that remote TLOC exists. If a tunnel exists and policy permits, the router will encapsulate and encrypt the original packet and send it toward the destination TLOC over the underlay. When the packet arrives, the remote edge validates the IPsec security association, decrypts the payload, removes the outer header, and forwards the inner packet to the destination on the local service-side VPN. A common misconception is to assume that control plane route presence guarantees traffic flow — without TLOC-level underlay reachability or an established tunnel, packets cannot traverse the overlay. Think of routes as directions and tunnels as the roads; you need both a direction and a usable road to reach the destination. How would you confirm both exist for a given prefix in your network?

keyIdea.text: Routes provide next-hop TLOCs; tunnels provide secure roads; both are required for the data plane to forward user traffic end to end.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › End-to-end Data Plane Flow
Core Concept

Packet journey explained

This explanation ties route information, TLOC selection, tunnel state, and final forwarding into a single operational picture.

FIB lookup
OMP populates routes; FIB maps prefixes to next-hop TLOCs used for forwarding decisions.
Tunnel existence
If no IPsec tunnel exists to the chosen TLOC, the router will negotiate it before sending encrypted traffic.
Decapsulation at destination
Destination edge decrypts and forwards the original inner packet based on local routing.
Key Takeaway

You need both route knowledge and an active tunnel between the specific TLOC IPs for live data forwarding.

Process Flow
1. Packet received
Original packet arrives on a service-side VPN interface.
2. FIB lookup
FIB gives next-hop TLOC for destination prefix, learned from OMP.
3. Tunnel check & encapsulate
Router ensures IPsec SA exists, then encrypts and wraps the packet with outer IP using TLOC IPs.
4. Underlay delivery & decap
Underlay routers forward outer IP. Destination edge decrypts and forwards inner packet to final host.
Concrete Example
Branch host 192.168.10.10 to DC host 172.16.20.1 — FIB points to TLOC 10.0.2.1
Once the tunnel to 10.0.2.1 is up, packets are encrypted and the underlay routes the outer header to that IP.
Common mistake
Assuming route presence = connectivity
You must verify underlay reachability to the TLOC IP and an active IPsec SA.

screens.title: FIB, OMP, and TLOC Selection
screens.narratorSegment: The control plane provides the information that populates the Forwarding Information Base, but it is the FIB that the edge uses to forward live traffic. OMP distributes prefixes and associates them with TLOC information. The FIB maps destination IP prefixes to the next-hop component — typically a remote TLOC IP — which the router uses when building the outer IP header for encapsulation. When multiple TLOCs are available for a destination, the FIB plus data-policy directives determine which TLOC is preferred in practice. This is where confusion often arises: someone may see multiple OMP routes and assume load sharing will happen automatically. In reality, the edge consults the FIB and any active data policy to make a single forwarding choice for each packet. A concrete example is a prefix learned from a data-center vEdge with both an MPLS and an internet TLOC. Control plane routes list both, but local policy may prefer MPLS for voice. To validate the decision, inspect the FIB and active data-policy hits on the edge; if traffic is still following the unintended path, check for a policy misapplication or a mismatch in TLOC labels that prevents the chosen tunnel from forming.

keyIdea.text: The FIB converts OMP route knowledge into a specific next-hop TLOC used by the data plane; policies can override or influence that choice.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › FIB, OMP, and TLOC Selection
Definition

From OMP to FIB

OMP provides prefixes and TLOC associations; the FIB stores the next-hop TLOC used by the data plane for each destination prefix.

Multiple TLOCs?
When multiple transport TLOCs exist, selection depends on FIB preference plus any active data policy like preferred-color or AAR decisions.
Mismatch pitfalls
Mismatched TLOC colors or encapsulation types can prevent expected tunnels, leaving a control-plane route unused by the data plane.
Key Takeaway

Confirm both FIB entries and that the TLOC IPs used by those FIB entries have reachable underlay paths and active SAs.

Architecture
Control plane
OMP distributes routes & TLOCs
vSmart advertises prefixes and the TLOCs that can reach them.
Data plane
FIB uses next-hop TLOC
Traffic is forwarded using the selected TLOC; encapsulation uses that TLOC's IP for the outer header.
Concrete scenario
Prefix 172.16.20.0/24 learned via OMP with TLOCs 10.0.2.1 (mpls) and 20.0.2.1 (biz-internet)
If data policy prefers mpls for voice, voice flows will choose 10.0.2.1; ensure that 10.0.2.1 is reachable in the underlay.

screens.title: IPsec Tunnel Establishment
screens.narratorSegment: IPsec tunnel establishment is the step that turns a route into a usable secure path. The edge initiates a tunnel when it needs to send traffic to a remote TLOC and no active SA exists. The two primary components are IKE for negotiating keys and authentication, and ESP for encrypting and validating the data packets. IKE negotiates the security association and key material; once SAs are in place, ESP provides confidentiality and integrity for the inner packet. In SD-WAN each TLOC can form multiple IPsec tunnels to matching remote TLOCs on different transports, giving resilience and path choice. A frequent troubleshooting misconception is to look only at higher-layer control-plane connectivity; if IKE cannot complete due to blocked UDP ports 500 or 4500, or NAT traversal failures, ESP SAs never form and traffic stalls even though OMP routes exist. When verifying tunnels, inspect both IKE state and IPsec SAs; they indicate whether negotiation finished and whether ESP protects traffic. If SAs exist but traffic still fails, confirm that the underlay routes to the TLOC IPs are functioning and that intermediate firewalls permit the negotiated traffic.

keyIdea.text: IKE negotiates keys and authentication; ESP provides the encryption and integrity that protects the inner packet during underlay transit.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › IPsec Tunnel Establishment
Definition

IKE then ESP

IKE negotiates the SA and keys. ESP uses that SA to encrypt and authenticate the inner packets between TLOCs.

Negotiation steps
IKE exchanges authentication and key material; both peers must complete it to create ESP SAs.
Multiple SAs
Each TLOC pair can have multiple IPsec tunnels across different underlay transports for redundancy and performance.
Key Takeaway

If IKE or ESP fails, tunnels will not carry traffic even when control-plane routes exist; check both SAs and underlay IP reachability.

Troubleshooting checklist
  • Verify UDP 500 and 4500 are permitted for IKE and NAT traversal.
  • Inspect IKE state with show crypto ikev2 sa to confirm negotiation completed.
  • Check ESP SAs with show crypto ipsec sa to confirm encryption is active.
  • Confirm underlay routes to both local and remote TLOC IPs exist.
Concrete example
Blocked UDP 4500
A firewall that blocks UDP 4500 will prevent NAT-T, causing IKE to fail and IPsec SAs not to form — resulting in no data plane tunnels.

screens.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation is the practical mechanism that lets the underlay carry encrypted SD-WAN traffic without understanding inner addressing. The edge router takes the original IP packet — headers and payload — encrypts it using the ESP SA, and then places that encrypted payload inside a new outer IP header whose source and destination are the local and remote TLOC IPs. The underlay network routes based only on that outer header. This preserves privacy and lets the overlay span arbitrary underlays. On arrival, the destination edge identifies the packet as IPsec-protected to one of its TLOC IPs, decrypts the ESP payload to recover the original packet, strips the outer header, and forwards the original to the final local destination. A common confusion is thinking intermediate underlay routers can inspect the original IP headers; they cannot because the inner payload is encrypted. For verification, you will often check the cEdge for counters showing encapsulated packets sent and decapsulated packets received, and verify ESP SA packet counters to confirm traffic is flowing over the tunnel. Encapsulation and Decapsulation Mechanics means outer header uses tloc ips and hides the inner packet; only the destination edge can decrypt and forward the original traffic.. In practical terms, what gets wrapped, encrypted, and why the underlay only sees tloc ips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Outer header uses TLOC IPs and hides the inner packet; only the destination edge can decrypt and forward the original traffic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Encapsulation and Decapsulation Mechanics
Process Flow

How encapsulation protects the inner packet

Original packet
Contains source/dest addresses and application payload from the service-side VPN.
ESP encryption
The original packet is encrypted to protect confidentiality and integrity.
Outer header
A new IP header with source and destination TLOC IPs wraps the encrypted payload for underlay routing.
Underlay visibility
Underlay routers route the outer IP without access to the encrypted inner packet. They only see TLOC-level endpoints.
Verification & counters
Check packet counters on the cEdge: encapsulated packet counters should increase on the sending side and decapsulated counters should increase on the receiving side. ESP SA packet counters confirm in-tunnel payloads are flowing.
Concrete example
Outer header: src TLOC 10.0.1.1 → dst TLOC 10.0.2.1
The underlay routes that outer packet by normal IP routing. The inner original IP remains hidden until the remote edge decrypts it.
Key Takeaway

Encapsulation lets SD-WAN traverse diverse underlays while keeping application traffic private and intact.

screens.title: TLOCs and Multiple Underlay Transports
screens.narratorSegment: A TLOC represents a transport location — a combination of IP, color, and encapsulation type that identifies how an edge connects to the underlay. Each TLOC can establish IPsec tunnels to matching remote TLOCs on the other edge, which means a single edge can maintain separate tunnels for MPLS, business internet, or direct internet connections simultaneously. This capability gives SD-WAN resilience and the ability to perform intelligent path selection. When an edge has multiple candidate TLOCs for a destination, selection is influenced by the FIB and data policies. For instance, voice traffic can be set to prefer an MPLS TLOC, while web traffic prefers the business internet TLOC but can fail over if performance degrades. A common error is misassigning colors or incorrect encapsulation types; such mismatches prevent tunnels from forming between the intended TLOC pair even though underlay routes exist. To validate behavior, verify that each transport’s TLOC IP is reachable, check IPsec connection entries for each TLOC pair, and review policy hits to see which TLOC the router actually used for a given traffic class. TLOCs and Multiple Underlay Transports means multiple tlocs let the fabric keep alternate secured paths; policy and health metrics decide the live tloc used for each traffic type.. In practical terms, why each transport builds its own ipsec tunnels and how the edge chooses between them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Multiple TLOCs let the fabric keep alternate secured paths; policy and health metrics decide the live TLOC used for each traffic type.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › TLOCs and Multiple Underlay Transports
Comparison

MPLS vs Internet TLOCs

Both are valid transports; each TLOC is identified by an IP and a color. Edges form IPsec tunnels between compatible TLOCs to create the overlay fabric.
MPLS TLOC
Typically preferred for low-latency or guaranteed SLA traffic such as voice.
Business Internet TLOC
Cost-effective path often used for general internet bound traffic and as a failover.
Key Takeaway

Ensure TLOC IP reachability and matching encapsulation to allow the desired tunnels to form across each transport.

Operational checks
  • Confirm each TLOC IP is reachable via underlay routing.
  • Verify IPsec connections exist between the expected TLOC pairs.
  • Check for color mismatches or encapsulation type differences that block tunnels.
Concrete example
Branch has mpls TLOC 10.0.1.1 and biz-internet 20.0.1.1; DC has matching TLOCs.
You will see separate IPsec connections for each pair in show sdwan ipsec connections and can select which to use via data policies.

screens.title: Data Policies: AAR, Service Chaining, QoS
screens.narratorSegment: Data policies operate in the data plane to directly influence forwarding decisions after the FIB lookup. They match traffic by attributes such as DSCP, application, or destination prefix, and then apply actions that affect path selection and service handling. Application-Aware Routing uses real-time link metrics — latency, loss, jitter — to choose between candidate TLOCs for specific flows, enabling scenarios such as preferring MPLS for voice when latency is low and failing over to internet when it is not. Service chaining steers traffic through network functions like firewalls or IPS before it reaches the destination. QoS actions mark or shape packets to prioritize critical applications. Policies are authored centrally and pushed to devices, but they execute locally on each edge, which means that incorrect match conditions or actions can cause traffic to be routed incorrectly or dropped. A practical example: a policy that matches DSCP EF for voice and sets preferred-color to mpls ensures voice uses the high-quality transport. To troubleshoot policy issues, inspect policy hit counters and test with traffic that matches the exact conditions used in the policy.

Core Concept

Policy-driven forwarding

Policies match traffic attributes and then set actions that change the forwarding path or apply services.

AAR
Chooses path based on loss, latency, jitter thresholds for the application.
Service Chaining
Steers traffic through a firewall, IPS, or other VNFs before delivery.
QoS
Marks and shapes traffic so critical flows get priority on egress.
Policy checks

  • Verify action semantics such as preferred-color or service-chain are correct for your topology.
  • Use policy hit counters to confirm enforcement on the edge.
Concrete example
Voice: match DSCP EF → set preferred-color mpls
This ensures voice flows try MPLS first; integrate AAR probes to trigger failover based on real-time link health.

Policies execute locally and can change forwarding immediately; always validate using hit counters and test traffic.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical policy design: ensure voice identified by DSCP EF uses MPLS when healthy, while general web traffic marked AF11 prefers business internet and can fail over to MPLS. Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Policy Example: Voice vs Web Traffic
Policy Example

Voice preferential routing with AAR

Two rule sets: one for voice with strict preferred-color mpls, one for web with preferred biz-internet and AAR for failover.

Match: DSCP EF
Action: set tloc-action preferred-color mpls and set qos/remarking as needed.
Match: DSCP AF11
Action: set tloc-action preferred-color biz-internet; enable AAR probes for failover to MPLS.
Key Takeaway

Policies must be validated with traffic tests and hit counters; AAR requires probe classes and thresholds to automate switching.

Validation steps
  1. Deploy policy to the target edges via vManage.
  2. Generate voice-like traffic and confirm policy hit counters increment for the voice rule.
  3. Simulate degraded biz-internet probe values and confirm AAR moves web flows to MPLS.
  4. Revert probes and confirm traffic returns to the preferred transport.
Concrete scenario
Voice uses MPLS when latency < 50ms; otherwise failover to internet
AAR probe classes must be configured for both transports and referenced by the data policy for automatic decisions.

screens.title: CLI Verification: Inspecting Tunnels and Traffic
screens.narratorSegment: Hands-on verification is essential. Start on the branch cEdge and run the command that lists IPsec connections to see remote TLOCs and their states. The command will show source and destination TLOC IPs, colors, remote site IDs, and whether the tunnel is up. If a tunnel is missing or down, the output reveals which TLOC pair lacks a connection. Next, inspect security associations: show crypto ipsec sa and show crypto ikev2 sa reveal whether ESP and IKE negotiations completed and include packet counters you can use to confirm live traffic. Then run ping and traceroute from the specific VPN context — for example, ping vpn 10 source — to test forwarding and observe whether the pings traverse the overlay. A successful ping with full packet replies plus incrementing ESP packet counters shows data plane forwarding is intact. If pings fail but control plane routes exist, prioritize checking underlay reachability between TLOC IPs and firewall rules that might block UDP 500/4500. This stepwise approach prevents you from chasing policy when the issue is simply a blocked port or missing underlay route.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › CLI Verification: Inspecting Tunnels and Traffic
Command Walkthrough

Verify tunnels and SAs

Run the following checks on Branch1 cEdge to confirm data plane health and traceability.

List IPsec connections
show sdwan ipsec connections
Inspect REMOTE TLOC IP and STATE columns for 'up'.
Check IPsec and IKE SAs
show crypto ipsec sa
show crypto ikev2 sa
Confirm ESP packet counters and IKE auth state; counters increasing indicate live traffic.
Ping and traceroute in VPN context
Example commands
ping vpn 10 172.16.20.1 source 192.168.10.1
traceroute vpn 10 172.16.20.1 source 192.168.10.1
These commands test forwarding from the specific service-side VPN so you exercise the exact path used by user traffic.
Interpreting output
If show sdwan ipsec connections shows 'up' and ping succeeds with responses, the data plane is working. If control plane routes exist but IPsec entries are missing, focus on underlay reachability and firewall port blocking for UDP 500/4500.

Work from tunnel presence to SAs to packet-level tests; correlate outputs to pinpoint the failure layer.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll follow real user traffic as it leaves a branch PC, moves into the local edge router, travels encrypted across the underlay, and arrives at a remote site. You will learn the essential pieces that make that journey possible: how the edge router finds the remote TLOC, how IPsec tunnels are negotiated, why encapsulation wraps the original packet for safe travel, and how data policies steer traffic for performance or security. Understanding this flow is critical for troubleshooting and for designing policies that preserve application experience. For example, you’ll see why a route in the control plane alone is not enough — the underlay must also carry the TLOC IPs so an IPsec tunnel can be established. We’ll also preview typical issues such as underlay reachability failure, firewall ports blocking IKE or NAT traversal, and policy misapplication that can lead to black-holing. By the end you will be able to explain the end-to-end forwarding path, verify IPsec state with CLI commands, and reason about policy-driven path choices.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace the full data plane path and explain why each step matters for secure, predictable forwarding. You will demonstrate understanding of IPsec tunnel establishment — how IKE negotiates keys and ESP protects packet integrity and confidentiality — and you will know how encapsulation uses TLOC IP addresses so the underlay can route encrypted traffic. You will also be able to read the device's forwarding information base and explain how an OMP-learned route becomes a next-hop TLOC in the FIB. Finally you will be comfortable describing how data policies influence live forwarding decisions, for example preferring an MPLS TLOC for low-latency voice or steering traffic through a firewall for inspection. Each objective ties to practical verification steps you can run on a cEdge to confirm that the overlay and tunnels are healthy.

These extended objectives focus on verification and troubleshooting. You will learn to identify common data plane problems such as underlay reachability failures, firewall rules blocking IKE or NAT traversal ports, and mismatched TLOC or color configurations. You will practice using the CLI to list IPsec connections, inspect IKE and ESP security associations, and run pings and traceroutes from a specific VPN context to confirm end-to-end forwarding. Finally, you will be able to reason about policy misapplication and how it can unintentionally drop or redirect traffic. Each objective connects to hands-on commands and expected output that let you validate the overlay without guessing. Learning Objectives — Extended means know the cli checks and expected behaviors that confirm tunnels, sas, and underlay reachability before changing policy or topology.. In practical terms, additional skills and verification steps. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start by picturing a host packet in a branch LAN that needs to reach a remote server in a data center VPN. The local cEdge receives the original packet and must determine how to forward it. That decision comes from the Forwarding Information Base, which maps destination prefixes to next-hop TLOC addresses learned from OMP via the control plane. The router looks up the prefix, selects the corresponding TLOC, and checks whether an IPsec tunnel to that remote TLOC exists. If a tunnel exists and policy permits, the router will encapsulate and encrypt the original packet and send it toward the destination TLOC over the underlay. When the packet arrives, the remote edge validates the IPsec security association, decrypts the payload, removes the outer header, and forwards the inner packet to the destination on the local service-side VPN. A common misconception is to assume that control plane route presence guarantees traffic flow — without TLOC-level underlay reachability or an established tunnel, packets cannot traverse the overlay. Think of routes as directions and tunnels as the roads; you need both a direction and a usable road to reach the destination. How would you confirm both exist for a given prefix in your network?

The control plane provides the information that populates the Forwarding Information Base, but it is the FIB that the edge uses to forward live traffic. OMP distributes prefixes and associates them with TLOC information. The FIB maps destination IP prefixes to the next-hop component — typically a remote TLOC IP — which the router uses when building the outer IP header for encapsulation. When multiple TLOCs are available for a destination, the FIB plus data-policy directives determine which TLOC is preferred in practice. This is where confusion often arises: someone may see multiple OMP routes and assume load sharing will happen automatically. In reality, the edge consults the FIB and any active data policy to make a single forwarding choice for each packet. A concrete example is a prefix learned from a data-center vEdge with both an MPLS and an internet TLOC. Control plane routes list both, but local policy may prefer MPLS for voice. To validate the decision, inspect the FIB and active data-policy hits on the edge; if traffic is still following the unintended path, check for a policy misapplication or a mismatch in TLOC labels that prevents the chosen tunnel from forming.

IPsec tunnel establishment is the step that turns a route into a usable secure path. The edge initiates a tunnel when it needs to send traffic to a remote TLOC and no active SA exists. The two primary components are IKE for negotiating keys and authentication, and ESP for encrypting and validating the data packets. IKE negotiates the security association and key material; once SAs are in place, ESP provides confidentiality and integrity for the inner packet. In SD-WAN each TLOC can form multiple IPsec tunnels to matching remote TLOCs on different transports, giving resilience and path choice. A frequent troubleshooting misconception is to look only at higher-layer control-plane connectivity; if IKE cannot complete due to blocked UDP ports 500 or 4500, or NAT traversal failures, ESP SAs never form and traffic stalls even though OMP routes exist. When verifying tunnels, inspect both IKE state and IPsec SAs; they indicate whether negotiation finished and whether ESP protects traffic. If SAs exist but traffic still fails, confirm that the underlay routes to the TLOC IPs are functioning and that intermediate firewalls permit the negotiated traffic.

Encapsulation is the practical mechanism that lets the underlay carry encrypted SD-WAN traffic without understanding inner addressing. The edge router takes the original IP packet — headers and payload — encrypts it using the ESP SA, and then places that encrypted payload inside a new outer IP header whose source and destination are the local and remote TLOC IPs. The underlay network routes based only on that outer header. This preserves privacy and lets the overlay span arbitrary underlays. On arrival, the destination edge identifies the packet as IPsec-protected to one of its TLOC IPs, decrypts the ESP payload to recover the original packet, strips the outer header, and forwards the original to the final local destination. A common confusion is thinking intermediate underlay routers can inspect the original IP headers; they cannot because the inner payload is encrypted. For verification, you will often check the cEdge for counters showing encapsulated packets sent and decapsulated packets received, and verify ESP SA packet counters to confirm traffic is flowing over the tunnel. Encapsulation and Decapsulation Mechanics means outer header uses tloc ips and hides the inner packet; only the destination edge can decrypt and forward the original traffic.. In practical terms, what gets wrapped, encrypted, and why the underlay only sees tloc ips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A TLOC represents a transport location — a combination of IP, color, and encapsulation type that identifies how an edge connects to the underlay. Each TLOC can establish IPsec tunnels to matching remote TLOCs on the other edge, which means a single edge can maintain separate tunnels for MPLS, business internet, or direct internet connections simultaneously. This capability gives SD-WAN resilience and the ability to perform intelligent path selection. When an edge has multiple candidate TLOCs for a destination, selection is influenced by the FIB and data policies. For instance, voice traffic can be set to prefer an MPLS TLOC, while web traffic prefers the business internet TLOC but can fail over if performance degrades. A common error is misassigning colors or incorrect encapsulation types; such mismatches prevent tunnels from forming between the intended TLOC pair even though underlay routes exist. To validate behavior, verify that each transport’s TLOC IP is reachable, check IPsec connection entries for each TLOC pair, and review policy hits to see which TLOC the router actually used for a given traffic class.
